sections.heading: What does a Marine Automation Engineer do?

blocks.text: A Marine Automation Engineer designs, maintains, tests and troubleshoots the automated electrical and control systems used aboard ships and in maritime facilities. The work helps keep propulsion-support systems, generators, pumps, alarms, navigation-support equipment and machinery monitoring systems operating safely.

The role may be shore-based or ship-based. A shipboard Electro-Technical Officer (ETO) is a regulated seafaring role with specific training, medical, sea-service and certification requirements. A general Marine Automation Engineer position does not automatically confer ETO eligibility.
Typical responsibilities

items.text: Maintain electrical distribution systems, motors, generators and switchboards.
Configure and troubleshoot programmable logic controllers (PLCs) and human-machine interfaces (HMIs).
Diagnose faults in sensors, actuators, alarms and machinery monitoring systems.
Support automation for pumps, ballast systems, fuel systems and auxiliary machinery.
Test electrical equipment and control circuits using appropriate instruments.
Maintain maintenance logs, technical drawings, spare-parts records and safety documentation.
Support equipment commissioning, planned maintenance and emergency fault response.
Follow electrical isolation, lockout/tagout and other applicable marine safety procedures.

blocks.text: Stage 1 — Build an electrical or electronics foundation

Consider a relevant engineering degree or diploma in Electrical, Electronics, Electronics and Communication, Instrumentation or another discipline accepted for the intended role and training programme.
Stage 2 — Learn industrial and marine automation
Develop practical skills in PLCs, electrical machines, instrumentation, control systems, troubleshooting and industrial communications.
Stage 3 — Choose the shipboard ETO route if desired
Check the current eligibility criteria for a DG Shipping-approved ETO course, including accepted prior qualifications, medical fitness, training and assessment requirements.
Stage 4 — Gain supervised technical experience
Build experience through eligible onboard training, ship-repair workshops, marine equipment companies, automation integrators or industrial maintenance teams.
The ETO route is regulated. The exact entry requirements depend on the applicable DG Shipping rules and the candidate's prior qualification.

According to DG Shipping's published ETO eligibility guidance, relevant electrical and electronics qualifications have been accepted for the conventional entry route. The authority has also published updated guidance in 2026, so candidates should verify the latest criteria before paying course fees.
Eligibility criteria
Before enrolling, verify:

items.text: Whether your diploma or degree discipline is accepted for the ETO course.
The required marks, age limits where applicable, English proficiency and medical fitness.
Whether the maritime training institute and specific course are currently approved.
The onboard training and sea-service requirements.
The examinations and Certificate of Competency requirements applicable to the intended route.

rows.text: Electrical engineering
AC/DC circuits, electrical machines, switchgear and protection
PLC programming
Ladder logic, inputs/outputs, interlocks and fault diagnosis
Instrumentation
Sensors, transmitters, calibration and signal conditioning
Control systems
Feedback loops, process control and PID fundamentals
Marine electrical systems
Generators, distribution boards, motors and emergency power
Industrial communication
Modbus, CAN-based systems and industrial Ethernet fundamentals
Troubleshooting
Reading schematics, testing circuits and identifying root causes
Safety
Electrical isolation, lockout/tagout, safe testing and emergency procedures
Technical documentation
Wiring diagrams, maintenance logs, fault reports and equipment manuals
Teamwork
Coordinating with engineering, electrical and shipboard operations teams

blocks.text: PLC and automation platforms
Siemens TIA Portal, Rockwell Studio 5000, Schneider EcoStruxure or equivalent platforms, depending on the employer and training lab.
Electrical testing equipment
Digital multimeter, clamp meter, insulation resistance tester and appropriate electrical test instruments under supervision.
HMI and SCADA
Operator interfaces, alarms, trends, data logging and supervisory monitoring.
Engineering documentation
Electrical CAD tools, wiring diagrams, equipment manuals, maintenance software and structured fault reports.
Tool familiarity is valuable, but employers may use different vendors and proprietary shipboard systems. Students should focus on transferable troubleshooting skills rather than a single brand.

blocks.label: Offshore automation
blocks.text: Electrical and instrumentation systems supporting offshore facilities, subject to role-specific requirements.
These projects are suitable for college laboratories or supervised training environments.
Project 1 — PLC-controlled bilge pump simulator
Simulate pump start/stop logic, high-level alarms, overload trips and manual override. Document the control sequence and fault conditions.
Project 2 — Generator monitoring dashboard
Build a simulated dashboard displaying voltage, current, frequency, temperature and alarm status using sample data.
Project 3 — Motor fault-diagnosis exercise
Prepare a supervised test plan for identifying common motor faults using simulated readings, wiring diagrams and appropriate instruments.
Project 4 — Engine-room alarm system
Create a PLC or software simulation for temperature, pressure and tank-level alarms, including alarm acknowledgement and event logging.
Project 5 — Preventive-maintenance tracker
Develop a spreadsheet or simple application for tracking equipment IDs, inspection dates, faults, spare parts and maintenance history.

For each project, retain a wiring diagram or block diagram, control logic, test cases, screenshots where appropriate, a fault log and a short explanation of the safety precautions. Never experiment on live shipboard equipment without authorisation and qualified supervision.
Investigate opportunities with:

items.text: Shipping companies offering approved ETO training or onboard placements.
Shipyards and marine electrical repair contractors.
Marine automation and instrumentation suppliers.
Industrial automation system integrators.
Port operators and cargo-terminal maintenance teams.
Offshore engineering and marine equipment service providers.
Electrical testing, commissioning and industrial maintenance firms.

blocks.text: Before accepting a shipboard training offer, verify the provider's approval status, training arrangement, onboard placement conditions and the applicable certification pathway. A general industrial internship can build technical skills, but it does not substitute for required maritime training or sea service.

Depending on prior qualifications and career goals, possible further-study areas include:

items.text: M.Tech or postgraduate study in electrical engineering.
Industrial automation and control systems.
Instrumentation and control engineering.
Marine engineering technology and maritime systems.
Power systems and electrical drives.
Robotics, industrial IoT and predictive maintenance.
Maritime operations or technical management.

blocks.text: These qualifications can strengthen technical specialisation, but do not independently qualify someone for a regulated ETO position.

items.text: Student / Engineering Trainee

blocks.text: Build foundations in electrical engineering, electronics, instrumentation and control systems.

items.text: Junior Automation or Electrical Engineer

blocks.text: Assist with PLC programming, testing, maintenance and fault diagnosis in a supervised role.

items.text: Marine Electrical / Automation Engineer

blocks.text: Handle increasingly complex marine equipment, commissioning, control systems and technical support.

items.text: Certified Electro-Technical Officer (shipboard route)

blocks.text: Undertake shipboard electrical and electronic duties within the scope of the required certification.

items.text: Senior Technical Specialist / Automation Lead

blocks.text: Potentially lead troubleshooting, commissioning, maintenance planning or technical teams with suitable experience.

items.text: Marine Automation Manager / Technical Superintendent

blocks.text: Potential long-term shore-based progression into technical management, subject to experience and employer requirements.

The shore-based engineering and shipboard ETO paths can overlap in technical knowledge, but they are not interchangeable. Progression depends on experience, competence, vacancies and applicable certifications.

blocks.label: Smart ships
blocks.text: Integrated monitoring, automated machinery and improved onboard data systems.

blocks.label: Predictive maintenance
blocks.text: Using equipment data to identify faults before failures occur.

blocks.label: Industrial cybersecurity
blocks.text: Protecting operational technology and shipboard control networks.

blocks.label: Remote diagnostics
blocks.text: Supporting vessel equipment from shore-based technical centres.

blocks.label: Energy efficiency
blocks.text: Monitoring electrical loads and improving the performance of marine systems.

blocks.label: Offshore electrification
blocks.text: Greater demand for capable electrical and control-system technicians across selected marine and offshore projects.
These are areas to explore, not guarantees of future employment or demand.

Reset checklist
A graduate preparing for this career should be able to:

items.text: Explain the operation of electrical machines, control circuits and marine automation systems.
Troubleshoot basic faults methodically and safely.
Understand PLCs, HMIs, sensors, alarms and machinery monitoring.
Produce clear technical reports and interpret electrical diagrams.
Work effectively with engineering teams and follow strict safety procedures.
Distinguish shore-based automation employment from the regulated shipboard ETO pathway.
Identify and complete the training, onboard service and certification requirements for the role they intend to pursue.

blocks.label: Recommended starting point
blocks.text: Build a strong electrical/electronics foundation, practise PLC and instrumentation projects, and verify the latest DG Shipping ETO eligibility rules before enrolling in maritime training.
